source: Sellier, Scopelliti, Morewedge (2019) Debiasing training transfers to improve decision making in the field (author manuscript, re-read for the 29% question)
finding: The manuscript abstract says trained students were 29% less likely to pick the hypothesis-confirming option. The results text gives 58.8% vs 72.2%, which is a 13.4 point drop and a relative risk of 0.81, not 0.71. The paper never shows how 29% was derived.
numbers: N=290. Raced: 58.8% trained vs 72.2% untrained, b=-.60, Wald chi2(1)=5.23, p=.022, exp(b)=.549, CI [.33,.92]. A different cell, the 4-day window, has exp(b)=.29 (b=-1.23, p=.024, CI [.10,.85]). Short lag 56.8% vs long lag 63.2%, p=.419.
quote: Trained participants were 29% less likely to choose the inferior hypothesis-confirming solution than untrained participants.
limits: The origin of 29% stays unproven. One possibility is that the .29 odds ratio of the 4-day window was read as a relative drop. This is a guess, not a finding. Quasi-experimental. The paper cites no independent replication.
agent_relevance: Quote the raw percentages (59% vs 72%), not 29%. Even the best human field result left 59% on the biased choice.

source: Heerma van Voss, Yoon, Scopelliti, Zweet, Helsloot, Morewedge (2025) Debiasing training reduces confirmation bias in national risk analysts, Scientific Reports
finding: A preregistered one-shot debiasing training lowered confirmation-bias scores in 71 national risk analysts and 118 master's students. Analysts started less biased than students. Training worked about equally for both.
numbers: Mixed ANOVA: intervention main effect F(1,169)=20.744, p<.001, partial eta2=.109; group effect F(1,169)=25.928, partial eta2=.133. ANCOVA pre to post: general domain F(1,168)=104.579, partial eta2=.384; risk domain F(1,168)=45.999, partial eta2=.215. Time x Group f=.023, p=.762. 56 of 71 analysts (78.9%) had complete data.
limits: Morewedge and Scopelliti are authors, so this is the same research programme, not an independent group. Pre/post design with no untrained control group. Test came right after training, so no retention or field transfer. Analyst sample is a convenience sample. Full text read via Europe PMC (PMC12660316).
agent_relevance: Gap 9 stays open. The only 2025 extension of the game result is from the same lab, and it measures survey items right after training.

source: Weber, Binder, Krauss (2018) Why can only 24% solve Bayesian reasoning problems in natural frequencies (Frontiers in Psychology); quotes McDowell and Jacobs (2017) meta-analysis
finding: The McDowell and Jacobs meta-analysis (Psychological Bulletin, 2017) is the baseline: natural-frequency wording lifts correct Bayesian answers to 24% vs 4% with probabilities, so most people still fail. In a new sample, many people re-converted frequencies into probabilities.
numbers: Meta-analysis figure as reported by the 2018 paper: 24% vs 4%. New study: 180 students, 360 inferences. Correct 20% (probability presentation) vs 36% (frequency presentation). 49% of people given frequencies still calculated with probabilities. Correct 61% when frequency calculation was used vs 9-13% with probability calculation.
limits: The meta-analysis itself was not opened, only its figures as quoted here (page read through a summariser, first 100,000 characters). Immediate tests of wording, not retention of training. Sedlmeier and Gigerenzer (2001) retention claim remains unchecked.
agent_relevance: Format change beats exhortation, but the 24% ceiling shows format alone is only partial. A scaffold step that restates a probability task as counts is a structure change, not an instruction.

source: Itzhak, Belinkov, Stanovsky (2025) Planted in Pretraining, Swayed by Finetuning (COLM 2025), re-read for scope
finding: Across 32 biases, models sharing a pretrained backbone had more similar bias patterns than models sharing instruction data. Seed noise was moderate. The two Itzhak papers conflict less than they look: 2024 showed instruction tuning shifts some biases, 2025 shows the overall pattern across biases is set by the backbone.
numbers: Bias-level clustering silhouette: by pretraining 0.028, random 0.014, K-means 0.104. Scenario-level: pretraining 0.066*, instruction 0.034*, random 0.006. Seed-mean vs original-model correlation 0.49 (OLMo) and 0.59 (T5). Same pattern on community Llama2-7B and Mistral-7B tuned on Tulu-2 or ShareGPT.
limits: Only OLMo-7B and T5-11B in the main test, LoRA and a downscaled Flan set. Supervised instruction tuning only. No RLHF, no preference optimisation, no reasoning RL, so gap 10 is NOT closed for 2025-2026 reasoning models.
agent_relevance: A scaffold cannot fix the backbone, so pick the backbone by measured bias profile. Do not assume post-training removed anchoring.

source: Sovrano, Dominici, Sevastjanova, Stramiglio, Bacchelli (2025) Is general-purpose AI reasoning sensitive to data-induced cognitive biases? PROBE-SWE (arXiv 2508.11278v2)
finding: Biased and unbiased wording of the same dilemma, matched in logic by Prolog. Every model flipped some decisions under the biased wording. Sensitivity rose with reasoning depth for 5 of 8 biases. Models often said they noticed the bias yet still flipped.
numbers: Six models: GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4.1-mini, GPT-4.1-nano, Llama-3.1-7B, Llama-3.3-70B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-70B. Mean sensitivity per bias from 5.9% (anchoring) to 35.3% (hindsight); overall 6-35%, up to 49% on harder items. 98.5% of 120 hand-checked dilemmas valid. Bias awareness about 0.5 (GPT-4.1 mini) to 0.8 (GPT-4o mini).
limits: Low-cost models, not 2026 frontier. Cues are still wording inside the prompt. Awareness is judged by an LLM that is the same model.
agent_relevance: Recognising a bias and resisting it are separate. Do not count a bias-aware sentence in the output as a pass; test the decision flip.

source: Sovrano, Dominici, Bacchelli (2026) Mitigating prompt-induced cognitive biases in general-purpose AI for software engineering (arXiv 2604.16756)
finding: On PROBE-SWE, standard prompts did not significantly cut bias per bias. Chain of thought made it worse. A two-step method that first has the model write the best practices for the decision and then answers cut sensitivity by about half.
numbers: Median sensitivity: control 12.9%; CoT 16.1%; implication prompt 13.3%; impersonated self-debias 10.2%; bias warning 10.3%; both warnings 8.3% (-4.6 points, no per-bias result significant after FDR, all p>=.07). Self-elicited axioms plus warning 6.3% (p<.001 after BH correction), axioms alone 7.2%. Per-model gains significant on gpt-4o-mini (3.7-3.8%) and DeepSeek-R1-distill (6.6-7.9%), not on gpt-4.1-nano or Llama. Anchoring not significant after FDR (p=.083). Hindsight got no help or worse. Rank-biserial .4-.5.
limits: Cheap models (about $500 run vs $3-8k for frontier). GPT-5.2 and Claude Opus 4.6 not tested. The extra generation step means more tokens than the control; no equal-token or best-of-N arm. Cue is still planted in wording.
agent_relevance: Closest thing to a scaffold-level debiaser beating plain prompting: make the model state the neutral rules first, then decide. Partly answers gaps 1 and 3 (warnings alone did not backfire here; they helped a little, not significantly). Equal-token test still missing.

source: Rios, Manrique, Quijano, Giraldo (2025) The Illusion of Rationality: tacit bias and strategic dominance in frontier LLM negotiation games (arXiv 2512.09254)
finding: Self-play bargaining with Claude Sonnet 4.5 and Gemini 2.5 Pro: the first offer strongly predicts the final price. Opening prices collapse onto round numbers (50, multiples of 5) instead of tracking the private valuation.
numbers: N=100 games per model. Spearman rho between opening and final normalised price: Claude Sonnet 4.5 0.78, Gemini 2.5 Pro 0.91. Temperature 0 vs 1: Gemini 0.90 to 0.92; Claude 0.71 to 0.90.
limits: No human baseline in the same task, so size is not comparable with Many Labs 2. Some link between opening and closing offer is rational in bargaining. Setup follows NegotiationArena.
agent_relevance: Frontier 2025 models still show an anchoring-like pattern in an agent-style multi-turn task. Anchoring is an agent risk, not only a quiz result.

source: Huang et al. (2026) Understanding the anchoring effect of LLM with synthetic data: existence, mechanism and potential mitigations (SynAnchors; v2, ICLR HCAIR workshop 2026)
finding: Anchoring appears in all tested models. Reasoning models are least anchored, but not zero. Mitigations tried on two 7-8B models gave at most about 10 points of relief.
numbers: Share of questions anchored: 22% to 61% across models; the lowest totals in Table 1 are 22.0% and 25.0%, which read as Qwen3-235B thinking and DeepSeek-R1. Text says human A-index is 0.4-0.6 and most LLMs are the same or worse. On Llama-3.1-8B (total 34.7%): question-aware prompt 36.8%, self-improving 38.4%, knowledge enhancement 50.5%, Anti-DP two-phase 24.7%. On Qwen2.5-7B (40.0%): question-aware 43.0%, self-improving 48.0%.
limits: Table 1 rows are misaligned in text extraction (mid-table rows do not match their labels), so model-level totals beyond the two lowest are not quoted. Mitigations tested only on small open models. Dataset built with DeepSeek-R1.
agent_relevance: Frontier reasoning models sit around 22-25% anchored items, lower than small models, not zero. A plain 'think carefully' reminder made the small models slightly worse. A two-phase 'set your standard first, then answer' step helped most.

source: Takenami, Huang, Murawaki, Chu (2025) How does cognitive bias affect LLMs? Anchoring in price negotiation simulations (arXiv 2508.21137)
finding: A buyer who is told that the seller is anchoring loses less. A reasoning buyer (o1, QwQ) lost less than a standard buyer only when informed. With no warning o1 lost as much as GPT-4o.
numbers: Buyer utility drop vs baseline when seller anchors, informed buyer in brackets: GPT-4o 0.38 (0.32); o1 0.40 (0.20); Qwen2.5 0.41 (0.20); QwQ 0.26 (0.00). GPT-4o buyer utility -0.04 at baseline, -0.41 under anchor. Paired t-tests, N=322 simulations. Personality traits did not correlate (|r| <= 0.10).
limits: The warning names a real planted manipulation by a counterpart, not a generic 'be unbiased'. The abstract says reasoning models are less prone; the table shows this mainly in the informed condition. Standard deviations are large (0.3-0.6).
agent_relevance: A specific, true warning plus thinking time works; a warning on a non-thinking model barely moves (0.38 to 0.32). Fits 4b: name the concrete cue, do not rely on a general instruction.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Assessing judging bias in large reasoning models: an empirical study (arXiv 2504.09946)
finding: DeepSeek-R1 and distilled R1 as judges are still swayed by bandwagon, authority, position and distraction cues. They lean toward the last option in preference tasks. A fake 'wait, let me think' phrase between options pushes them further toward later options. Better than non-reasoning models on factual items.
numbers: Mitigation, abstract: targeted system prompt up to 19% (preference sets) and 14% (fact sets); in-context examples up to 27% on preference sets, inconsistent on facts; self-reflection up to 10% (preference) and 16% (fact). On the Chemistry set self-reflection gave about 8% average gain on bandwagon; the system prompt gave a 2% decline on bandwagon in one setting.
limits: Judges: DeepSeek-R1, R1-70B, GPT-4o and others. No o3 or GPT-5. 'Up to' numbers are best cases. Biases are planted in the prompt.
agent_relevance: Reasoning-style filler can itself be a bias lever. Strip phrases like 'wait, let me think' from candidate answers before a judge sees them.

source: Wang, Lou, Tang, Chen, He (2026) Chain-of-Models: cross-model auditing for bias-robust LLM judges (arXiv 2607.28636)
finding: A second model that audits the first model's reasoning trace before the verdict beats no audit. The best auditor depends on the bias, and a strong standalone model is not necessarily a strong auditor.
numbers: Qwen2.5-72B alone 0.805 mean accuracy over four planted biases; best fixed auditor (GPT-4o) 0.824; per-bias selector 0.884. Sycophancy: baseline 0.655, GLM-5 auditor 0.890 (+23.5 points), GPT-4o auditor 0.640 (below baseline). Kimi-K2.5 is best standalone on bandwagon/authority/distraction (0.875/0.820/0.970) but as auditor gives 0.400 and 0.500 on bandwagon and authority. Bandwagon: baseline 0.830, GPT-4o auditor 0.887. Test split 25 items per cell.
limits: Cues planted in the prompt and the bias type assumed known. The chain roughly doubles latency; the paper says the cost is latency, not tokens, but has no equal-compute best-of-N arm. Small cells.
agent_relevance: Supports a different-family checker step with a known-cue prompt. Does not show benefit against biases the author did not plant, so gap 1 stays open.

source: Shi et al. (2025) Judging the Judges: a systematic study of position bias in LLM-as-a-Judge (arXiv 2406.07791v9)
finding: Position bias is not chance, differs by judge and task, depends little on length and mostly on how close the two answers are in quality.
numbers: 15 judges, MT-Bench and DevBench, 22 tasks, about 40 answer models, over 150,000 evaluations. Position consistency (pairwise, MT-Bench): GPT-4 0.82, Llama-3.3-70B 0.80, GPT-4o 0.76, GPT-3.5-Turbo 0.70, Gemini-1.5-pro 0.62. List-wise: GPT-4o 0.68, GPT-3.5 0.34. Repetition stability 0.90-1.00 for the top judges. GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 prefer the later answer on MT-Bench but the earlier one on DevBench.
limits: Judges up to GPT-4o, o1-mini, Claude-3.5 (Claude row values not used because the table text is garbled). No 2026 judges. Consistency 0.82 means about 18% of pairs change on swap.
agent_relevance: Swap-and-aggregate is needed for judge steps even with top judges, and costs two calls per pair; the bigger the quality gap, the less it matters.

source: Ye et al. (2024) Justice or Prejudice? Quantifying biases in LLM-as-a-Judge (CALM, arXiv 2410.02736)
finding: Twelve judge biases were tested by principled edits. Position, verbosity, self-enhancement and others persist in strong judges. Position bias grows with the number of candidates.
numbers: Robustness rate for position: ChatGPT 0.566, GPT-4-Turbo 0.818, GPT-4o 0.776, Claude-3.5 0.832, Qwen2 0.760. With three or four candidates most models score below 0.5. Bandwagon: GPT-4o 0.791, Claude-3.5 0.610. Authority: GPT-4o 0.787, Claude-3.5 0.865. Self-enhancement present even when answers are anonymised.
limits: Edited cues partly generated with GPT-4o. 2024 models.
agent_relevance: Keep judge steps to pairs and randomise order. Use a different model to judge than to generate.

source: Kumar, Rathore, Moitra (2026) All verdicts are not equal: rethinking LLM judge reliability (arXiv 2610.12083)
finding: Six judges, including GPT-5.2, Gemini-2.5-Pro and Claude-Sonnet-4.6, still change verdicts across identical reruns and across order swaps. Format and task swing reliability more than judge identity.
numbers: 7-17% of verdicts change across identical replications at temperature 0; up to 98% flip on order swap (Gemini-2.0-Flash, JudgeBench, verdict-first XML; accuracy 51.0% equals the ceiling 1 - flip/2, trustworthy rate T=2.0%). JudgeBench direct prompt, order-flip rate: GPT-5.2 11.0%, Claude-Sonnet-4.6 14.9%, GPT-4o 24.0%, Gemini-2.5-Pro 56.0%. Gemini-2.5-Pro T 28.9% (direct) to 77.5% (verdict-first JSON), 77.9% with one-call rubric scoring. FLASK four-call rubric decomposition lowered T for five of six judges versus direct.
limits: Pairwise only, English, closed-weight, four benchmarks. T combines three failure types.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 7: position bias persists in 2026 judges but varies hugely by model and prompt format. One-call rubric scoring beat four-call decomposition, so more calls do not buy reliability. Measure flip rate per judge before trusting it.

source: Chae, Kim, Jung, Choi, Jung (2026) Self- and other-labels induce bidirectional bias in LLM judges (arXiv 2608.18091v3)
finding: With style removed from the task, real self-preference vanishes in blind judging. But a self-label raises scores and an other-label lowers them, whatever the true author.
numbers: Ten judges incl. Claude Opus 4.7, GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Grok 4.3, DeepSeek-V4-Pro. Mixed model, average score on a 7-point rubric: label effect +0.43 (CI .39 to .47, p<.001); true-source effect +0.02 (p=.689); interaction -0.01. Per-judge change from blind: Gemini 3.1 Pro self +0.302 / other -0.444; Claude Opus 4.7 self +0.275 / other -0.023; GPT-5.5 self -0.019 / other -0.340.
limits: One task type (narrative constraint selection). Two judges had too little score range. Label effect, not self-recognition.
agent_relevance: Do not tell a judge which agent wrote an answer. Hide source labels in any critique step.

source: Guey and Bougault (2026) Self-preference is weak or absent in verifiable instruction-following revision (arXiv 2606.20093)
finding: When a deterministic checker decides which fix is good, authors reject verified-good fixes to their own drafts about as often as a fresh model does.
numbers: Four mid-tier model families, 85 author-vs-fresh comparisons on IFEval. Gap -5.1 points, CI [-12.9, +2.7]. 97% of stated rejection reasons were flaw-catching. Effects below 13 points cannot be excluded.
limits: Small and underpowered. Mid-tier models. Verifiable task only. Abstract and introduction read.
agent_relevance: Self-review of checkable output may not carry self-preference; the risk is larger for open-ended judging. Narrows d15.

source: Weerasekara, Kamarthi, Isaacs (2026) Conditional cognitive biases in LLMs: biased user turns modulate in-context reasoning (arXiv 2608.05166), re-read for gap 8
finding: Adding any preceding user turn raises measured bias, even a neutral one. A biased turn then partly lowers bias again by triggering alignment-style suppression in most models. Two models with chain-of-thought or constitutional training behaved differently.
numbers: 24,300 prompts, 9 x 9 bias matrix, 8 models. Zero-shot bias 0.342-0.437. Neutral turn effect +0.086 (Llama-3.1-8B, t=13.31), +0.061 (Llama-3.1-70B), -0.101 (Claude-3.5-Haiku). Biased-turn total effect +0.022 to +0.051 in 6 of 8. Content effect: -0.035 (Llama-8B; 30.6% of rows suppressed vs 26.4% amplified), +0.037 (Claude-3.5-Haiku). Planning fallacy rose in every model.
limits: User turns only, not tool outputs or the agent's own history. 2024-vintage models. No pruning experiment, so removal by pruning is untested.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 is half closed: bias is measurable and depends on context format. Whether code that prunes or neutralises context removes it is untested. Test on our own agent loop.

source: Zhuang et al. (2025) Alleviating choice-supportive bias in LLM with reasoning dependency generation (arXiv 2512.03082)
finding: Fine-tuning on balanced reasoning pairs that decouple the choice from the evidence lowered choice-supportive bias without hurting BBQ scores. It needs training, so it is not available to a scaffold-only agent.
numbers: Abstract: 81.5% improvement in memory-based experiments and 94.3% in the evaluation-based experiment; similar BBQ performance.
limits: Only the abstract and introduction were read in detail. Fine-tuning. Improvement is defined against the authors' baseline.
agent_relevance: Choice-supportive bias (praising the option you picked) is a real agent risk after a plan step. A scaffold analogue is to score options before choosing and not to rewrite the case for the chosen one afterwards. Untested.

source: Getting out of the Big-Muddy: escalation of commitment in LLMs (2025, arXiv 2508.01545)
finding: Alone, LLMs show little escalation of commitment. In peer groups and under compound pressure the bias is large. Bias depends on social context.
numbers: N=6,500 trials. Individual decisions (N=4,000): minimal escalation. Multi-agent: asymmetric hierarchy 46.2%, symmetric peers 99.2% (N=500). Compound pressure (N=2,000): 68.95% average allocation to the failing division.
limits: Model names not found in the extract; abstract-level numbers only. Roles are set by prompt.
agent_relevance: Multi-agent setups with equal peers can create near-universal escalation. A single-agent design avoids that; an internal critic should not be a deferring peer.
